title: Class 11 Chemistry — Foundation and Fundamentals Study Guide
notes: Chemistry explains the composition, structure, properties and transformations of matter, connecting microscopic atoms, ions and molecules with measurable properties. Physical chemistry studies principles and measurements; inorganic, organic and applied chemistry organize substances and practical uses.

An atom retains the chemical identity of an element. A molecule is a discrete bonded group; ionic compounds are described by formula units. Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) and relative molecular/formula mass (Mᵣ) are ratios to one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom and are dimensionless. Molar mass has units g mol⁻¹ and is numerically equal to the corresponding relative mass.

One atomic mass unit, u (or amu), is one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. In school-level formulae, a radical is an atom or group of atoms that behaves as a unit and carries charge, such as NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻ or NO₃⁻. Write cations first, balance total charge, and use parentheses when a polyatomic ion occurs more than once.

A molecular formula gives actual atom counts (C₆H₁₂O₆); an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio (CH₂O). Reduce subscripts by their greatest common divisor. If molar mass is known, multiply the empirical formula by n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass.

Mass percent of element X = (mass of X in one formula unit ÷ Mᵣ of compound) × 100%. For C₆H₁₂O₆, Mᵣ = 180 and carbon contributes 72/180 × 100 = 40.0%. Percentages should total approximately 100%; small differences can result from rounding.

Worked empirical-formula method: assume 100 g when percentages are given, convert each element's mass to moles, divide by the smallest amount, and scale to whole numbers. For 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O, the mole ratio is approximately 3.33:6.7:3.33 = 1:2:1, giving CH₂O.
Exam checks: distinguish dimensionless relative mass from molar mass in g mol⁻¹; verify ionic neutrality and simplest ratios; keep units in calculations and round only at the end.
formulas: % by mass of X = (mass of X in one formula unit ÷ Mᵣ) × 100%
Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass
keyPoints: Relative masses are ratios without units; molar mass is expressed in g mol⁻¹.
Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula gives actual atom counts.
Use ion charges to form neutral ionic formulae and reduce subscripts to the simplest ratio.
Check percentage totals and state units in numerical answers.
practiceQuestions: Explain why relative molecular mass is dimensionless while molar mass has units.
Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in CaCO₃ using Ca = 40, C = 12 and O = 16.
Write the formulae of aluminium sulfate and ammonium phosphate from their ion charges.
A compound has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 56 g mol⁻¹. Determine its molecular formula.
summary: Read formula subscripts, calculate relative masses, use ion charges to write neutral formulae, and distinguish empirical from molecular formulae.
